label: paragraph_title
text: Hongkong, Thursday; May. 6, 1926.

label: paragraph_title
text: NO ADVANCE.

label: text
text:
From the voluminous reports of the events of the second day of the general strike at Home, it will be seen that no advance has been made toward a resumption of the negotiations which so unhappily broke down at the last moment.
The only verdict possible on the whole miserable business is that volunteered by an American newspaper, which describes it as a tragedy. That it undoubtedly is. The only ray of hope comes from the House of Commons, where all Parties in the debate on the emergency regulations appeared most anxious to assist in the search for a formula on the basis of which the negotiations could be resumed. Even a typical Labourite emphasized the need for resumption, lest the action of some hot-heads might precipitate a catastrophe. Moreover, some light on the situation was thrown by the Labour member for Derby, Mr. J. H. Thomas, who was one of the Negotiating Committee of the Trades Union Congress, who revealed that the Labourites had a formula prepared for presenta

label: text
text: tion to the Prime Minister when the negotiations were so precipitately broken off. That disclosure has created quite a stir in political circles, and there is bound to be an urgent demand for popular curiosity as to the nature of the formula to be satisfied.

label: text
text: ment, through the Earl of Birkenhead, in the House of Lords, has firmly ruled that there can be no possible question of resuming the negotiations so long as the threat of the general strike holds the field. In this decision the Government will assuredly be most strongly supported by the mass of public opinion. That threat of a general strike was a deplorable error of judgment on the part of the Labourites at the most critical moment of the negotiations which at one stage promised so well. As Mr. Lloyd George said in effect in the House of Commons yesterday that the general strike has obscured the merits of the miners' case. He might have gone further and declared that the miners' case has been swamped altogether so far as public interest both within and without the United Kingdom, is concerned. The Trade Unionists have ranged themselves against the whole nation, and they cannot complain if by so doing they have jeopardised the miners' case and alienated the sympathies of thousands. No great heed may be paid to the reports of disturbances in various parts of the country. It was only to be expected that in the first stage of a general strike many of the unruly elements would be let loose and imagine that by lawless acts against tramcars and omnihouses they have made of themselves veritable heroes. They will soon find that respect for the law is essential in their own interests, for the forces of the Crown are more than sufficient to cope with all the hotheads and intimidators, as was proved last year even in the small Colony of Hongkong. Summed up, it may safely be declared that although nothing tangible is reported in the direction of a truce, the position is not yet irretrievable.

label: text
text: Amongst the passengers who left by the President Jefferson were Mrs. A. H. Compton and Mr. A. H. Rowe.

label: paragraph_title
text: PROVINCIAL DISORDERS

label: text
text:
Mrs. Goillin, of No. 3, Mody Road, Kowloon, reported to the Water Police yesterday that she had lost from a drawer in her bedroom bank notes to the value of $400. She suspected a house-boy she had dismissed. The theft took place sometime between Tuesday noon and yesterday morning.
Serious Attacks on Trams and

label: text
text: According to unofficial reports from the provinces the most disorderly place so far is glasgow, where mounted police were called out in the Parkhead district to epel attacks on trancars and notor buses.

label: text
text: One tramway, inspector was hauled off a car and assaulted so badly that he had to be taken to hospital.

label: text
text: The windows of another car were smashed, but the passengers escaped injury.

label: text
text: Omnibuses in the Renfrewshire district had to be withdrawn after a number were forced to speed up and escaped from their pursuing assailants.

label: text
text: Reports of cars being overturned have been received from Renfrew and Nottingham, whilst in Dundee the Manager of the tramways tried to run a car but the strikers blocked the line and the car was abandoned.

label: text
text: In Nottingham the strikers seized the carburetters and poured out the petrol of omnibuses worked by volunteers.

label: text
text:
A Baton Charge.
A crowd of 6,000 at Stoke-on-Trent, to-day stoned an omnibus, which the police were protecting, breaking the windows. The police charged with their batons, injuring a number. There were five arrests.

label: text
text: It is estimated that 100 trancars and omnibuses are operating in Edinburgh, being worked mostly by students.

label: text
text: Riotly per cent. of the tramway employees in Portsmouth resumed, when they were threatened with dismissal.

label: text
text: Extra Police were drafted into Newcastle and soon quelled attacks on the motor buses.

label: text
text:
Destroyers have arrived at Newcastle and Middlesbrough.
The battleship Hood and the cruisers Warspite and Comus have arrived on the Clyde.

label: text
text: The Comus is proceeding upriver from Greenock.

label: text
text: Reports from the mining area of South Wales depict that life is normal. The miners are working in their gardens or playing football, cricket, and quoits.

label: text
text: Owing to the Stepney Borough Trade Council calling out the day employees of the Municipal electric works the London Hospital was deprived of light and power yesterday. The X-ray work and electrical treatment were consequently suspended.

label: text
text: The power facilities were restored in the evening, the ban apparently applying to the day shift only.

label: text
text: "Daily Mail" Repeats Leading Article.

label: text
text: The "Daily Mail" appeared in the afternoon in the shape of a penny photographed typewritten news sheet printed on both sides. It includes Monday's leading article: "For King and Country," the refusal of the workers to print which led to the non-publication of Monday's "Daily Mail."

label: text
text: A column editorial to-day is headed: "Looking to Baldwin to act." It says that the lawful Government must act strongly and its opponents will collapse very quickly. It refers to Italy as an example of a Virile Western Government.

label: text
text:
A new feature in London is the appearance of a flood of little job-printed handbill newspapers, which are selling like hot cakes at threepence each. The news is mostly stale, being a repetition of the broadcast bulletin and the Chester racing results.
The postal authorities announce that the telephones and telegraphs are so congested that the calls on the wires must be reduced to a minimum.
"Midnight" at Noon!
An extraordinary pall of darkness like midnight spread over London at noon, intensifying the traffic congestion. Fortunately it soon lifted.
Irish Communications.
Malls between the Irish Free State and Great Britain are suspended.
Sallings between Holyhead and Dublin are cancelled.
The Cross Channel Dover-Calais service is functioning with one stemmer each day.
No trains are moving in Carlisle. Passengers arriving there from London are taken to Edinburgh in
Coventry is flooded with orders for bicycles from London, which it is unable to fulfil.

label: text
text: It appears in regard to the disorders in Newcastle that the crowd stoned the motor buses at Wallsond-on-Tyne yesterday evening. Two workmen were medically treated. The omnibus drove on knocking down two or three strikers.

label: text
text: An unusual feature is that the London electric trains are being driven by men attired in plus fours and golf caps.

label: text
text: A humorous incident occurred in Eccleston Square. An Ex-Service Men's Association Band entered the north side playing: Land of Hope and Glory. It proceeded to the west side, where are the headquarters of the Trade Unions Congress and struck up "The Red Flag" being greeted with showers of coppers from the windows.

label: paragraph_title
text: GLASGOW CARS.

label: paragraph_title
text:
A Decided Improvement
Reported.

label: text
text: There is an improvement in Glasgow to-day in the tramway situation. It is announced that 114 tramcars are running. There is also a slight improvement in the railway services.

label: text
text: An emergency news sheet appeared in Glasgow as the result of the morning and evening newspapers joining editorial forces.

label: text
text:
Half the railway services are
running in Liverpool.

label: paragraph_title
text: A NEW INTEREST

label: paragraph_title
text: Profittering News Boys

label: text
text:
Listless groups of strikers and street corner loafers in London get a new interest in life with the appearance of news boys, who have found a lucrative substitute for newspapers by selling single-sheet racing and cricket results, for which a "profiteering charge of threepence" is made.
The "Evening Standard" was on sale in the West-end to-night, the proprietors devoting the receipts to charity.

label: text
text: A few sporadic cases of rioting have so far occurred but have been speedily handled by the administration of batons which the Police evidently consider more efficacious than a prosecution for the type of individual involved.

label: paragraph_title
text: SEDITIONS!

label: paragraph_title
text: Jall for Company Director.

label: text
text: A prosecution—the first under the Emergency Powers Act—was held in Manchester, William Stoker, described as a company director, being sentenced to two months' imprisonment in the second division for an "act calculated to cause disaffection amongst the Forces and civilians."

label: text
text: It was stated that Stoker's high-powered car was standing outside the Socialist Hall at Openshaw ready to convey to Glasgow 1,600 copies of the Workers' daily, which, the prosecution alleged, Stoker knew contained seditious matter. Notice of an appeal was given.

label: text
text: The latest disturbances occurred in Albert Square, Manchester, where the Police dispersed a large demonstration of unemployed, also in West London and South-East London, where attempts were made to prevent buses running. The Police restored order. They have the situation well in hand everywhere, though heavy calls are made on their alertness to prevent the crowds who were dispersed forming again elsewhere.

label: text
text: The Trades Union Congress, in one of their few communiques, say that in the course of instruction given to the Unions they emphasised as essential the industrial nature of the dispute

label: text
text: The congress claim that resolutions have been received from the French, Dutch, American, Canadian and Irish movements promising to do their utmost to bring the matter to a successful issue.

label: text
text:
Publication Sanctioned.
After some hours the Police sanctioned the printing of the "British Worker", which consists of eight sheets of the size of Punch.
It contains a special message to the workers from the Trades Union Congress emphasising that this is an industrial dispute and urging exemplary conduct. It specially asks pickets to avoid obstruction.

label: text
text:
Protection Assured.
An official notice has been issued to the printing trade, bespeaking the intention of the Government to insist on the inclusion in any settlement of a clause preventing Trade Unions victimising any man remaining at work or resuming work during the dispute, and adding that men doing their duty to the country in the present crisis will not be left unprotected from subsequent reprisals.

label: paragraph_title
text: "VERY REASSURING."

label: text
text: Position Summed Up Last Night.

label: text
text: The official view to night is very reassuring and that the railway service is much better than the second day of any previous strike affecting the railways, whilst a general improvement is being made, for instance, at Liverpool where 1,000 young men are organised into squads to assist in any way they may be required.

label: text
text:
The opinion is expressed that
ample Forces are available to main-
tain law and order.

label: text
text: Supplies of fuel and food are regarded as sufficient to sustain life though not prosperity, for several weeks.

label: text
text: A pleasing feature is the fortitude and good temper shown by the bulk of the population.

label: paragraph_title
text: IRISH ACTION

label: text
text: Powers to the Governor:

label: text
text: The Northern Ireland Parliament has passed a Government Bill empowering the Governor, if an emergency arises, to proclaim a state of emergency and regulate the supply and distribution of the necessities of life.

label: paragraph_title
text:
IN THE COMMONS.
Debate on the Emergency Powers.

label: text
text: In the House of Commons, Sir W. Joynson Hick, Secretary of State for Home Affairs, moving the confirmation of the Emergency Power Regulations, quoted the declarations made by Mr. Ramsay MacDonald in 1924 in support of these, which were a very fair statement of the present Government's position.

label: text
text:
He explained that the regulations against incitement to mutiny and disaffection enabled summary action to be taken instead of a long trial. The Police were authorised to arrest without a warrant.
Another regulation enabled a search to be made of any building suspected of printing or issuing a document calculated to cause mutiny or disaffection among the Crown Forces, Police, or civilians, or to impede or restrict measures for water, fuel, light, and other public necessities.

label: text
text:
This regulation gave him great power, but he said quite definitely that in the interests of the life of the nation these powers were at present necessary.
